Carolina Crossroads: A $2.08 Billion Fix for “Malfunction Junction”

The Carolina Crossroads project is a $2.08 billion SCDOT initiative reconfiguring 14 miles of the I-20/I-26/I-126 corridor in Columbia — the interchange complex long known as “Malfunction Junction.” More than 134,000 vehicles daily pass through this corridor, making it the busiest interchange system in South Carolina. Construction began in November 2021 with a target completion in the mid-2030s, meaning drivers and truckers will navigate active construction for more than a decade.

The project is projected to save commuters 112 hours annually when complete. But until then, the corridor is a shifting maze of closed ramps, temporary lane configurations, new bridges under construction, and unfamiliar routing — all carrying the same massive traffic volume through a progressively constricted space. For the thousands of commercial trucks that transit the I-20/I-26 interchange daily, the construction zone creates conditions where crashes are more likely and more dangerous.

Recent Fatal and Serious Crashes in the Carolina Crossroads Zone

May 2025: Fatal Rear-End Crash on I-26

In May 2025, a driver was killed after rear-ending a Mack truck on I-26 near mile marker 122 at approximately 3:00 a.m. Rear-end crashes with commercial trucks are among the most deadly collision types because of the massive weight differential. In a construction zone with concrete barriers and no shoulders, a passenger vehicle that strikes the rear of a stopped or slow-moving truck has no escape path. The 3:00 a.m. timing suggests the victim may not have seen the truck in time — construction zone lighting, reflective tape on the truck's rear, and work zone sight distances are all factors that determine whether a driver can detect and avoid a stopped truck.

Permanent Ramp Closures Create Driver Confusion

In November 2024, SCDOT permanently closed the I-26 off-ramp to Bush River Road as part of the Carolina Crossroads reconfiguration. Permanent ramp closures — as opposed to temporary lane shifts — fundamentally change the routing that drivers and truckers have relied on for decades. GPS systems may not update immediately, sending truck drivers toward closed ramps where sudden braking and last-second lane changes create rear-end and sideswipe hazards. The Bush River Road corridor already handles heavy truck traffic from nearby distribution centers and commercial properties.

Phase 2 Completion: New Bridges and Shifting Traffic

Phase 2 of the project, which included work on I-20 at Broad River Road and the construction of three new bridges, was completed in early 2025. Each phase completion brings relief to one section of the corridor but shifts construction activity — and its associated hazards — to the next section. Drivers who have adapted to one set of lane configurations must now learn a new one. The I-26/I-20/I-77 interchange area remains one of the most complex navigation challenges for commercial truckers in the Midlands.

Why Carolina Crossroads Is Dangerous for Truck Traffic

134,000+ Daily Vehicles Through Active Construction

The I-20/I-26/I-126 corridor carries more than 134,000 vehicles per day, including thousands of commercial trucks serving Columbia's warehousing, manufacturing, and distribution industries. The construction zone does not reduce this traffic volume — it compresses it into fewer lanes with tighter margins. During peak hours, the combination of congestion, construction barriers, and truck traffic creates stop-and-go conditions where rear-end crashes are inevitable.

A Multi-Year Timeline of Shifting Configurations

With construction running from 2021 into the mid-2030s, truckers who use this corridor regularly face years of shifting lane configurations. A driver who transited the interchange last month may find entirely different lane alignments, ramp locations, and merge points on the next trip. This constant change is particularly dangerous for commercial truck drivers who rely on muscle memory and route familiarity to navigate complex interchange systems at highway speeds.

Nighttime Construction and Reduced Visibility

Much of the Carolina Crossroads work occurs at night to minimize daytime traffic disruption. The May 2025 fatal crash at 3:00 a.m. occurred during these nighttime construction hours when visibility is reduced, temporary lane markings may be less visible, and construction equipment may be operating near travel lanes. Truck drivers operating during nighttime hours may be fatigued, further reducing reaction times in an already hazardous environment.

What to Do After a Truck Crash in the Carolina Crossroads Zone

  1. Call 911 immediately — South Carolina Highway Patrol responds to crashes on the I-20/I-26/I-126 corridor. If you are in the construction zone with no shoulder, stay in your vehicle with seatbelt fastened and hazard lights on.
  2. Document the work zone: Photograph construction signage, speed limit signs, barrier placement, ramp closure signs, lane markings, and any construction equipment near the crash scene. These conditions change frequently.
  3. Record the truck: Company name, USDOT number, trailer number, and cargo type.
  4. Get medical treatment: Prisma Health Richland Hospital is Columbia's Level 1 trauma center. Get evaluated even if you feel fine — rear-end crashes with commercial trucks frequently cause traumatic brain injuries and spinal cord injuries with delayed symptoms.
  5. Contact a truck accident attorney within 24–48 hours — ELD data, event data recorder information, construction zone traffic control plans, and dash cam footage must be preserved before the trucking company or SCDOT can alter them.

  • Comparative fault: South Carolina allows recovery if you are less than 51% at fault. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault.
  • SC Tort Claims Act: Claims against SCDOT are subject to the SC Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-80), which imposes damage caps and procedural requirements. Filing deadlines for government claims may be shorter than the standard statute of limitations.

Bush River Road & I-26: Lexington County's Most Dangerous Truck Intersection

The intersection of Bush River Road and I-26 is the most dangerous intersection in Lexington County. This interchange sits at the western edge of Columbia's notorious "Malfunction Junction" — the I-20/I-26 interchange complex that is one of the most dangerous highway convergences in South Carolina. When heavy commercial truck traffic from I-26, I-20, and Bush River Road's commercial corridor converges at this location, the result is a sustained pattern of severe and fatal crashes.

Lexington County recorded 8,162 total collisions and 46 fatal crashes in 2023. The Bush River Road/I-26 interchange and the adjacent Malfunction Junction account for a disproportionate share of those crashes.

SCDOT Permanently Closes I-26 Off-Ramp to Bush River Road

In November 2024, SCDOT permanently closed the westbound I-26 off-ramp to Bush River Road as part of the Carolina Crossroads improvement project. This closure was a direct acknowledgment that the interchange design was fundamentally unsafe. However, the closure itself creates new hazards: trucks that previously exited at Bush River Road must now use alternative exits and navigate unfamiliar surface roads to reach their destinations. Drivers unfamiliar with the new traffic patterns make unexpected lane changes and turns, and increased volume at adjacent interchanges creates secondary crash hotspots.

Malfunction Junction: I-20/I-26 Interchange

The I-20/I-26 interchange — known locally as "Malfunction Junction" — is the hub of Columbia's interstate system and one of the most dangerous highway interchanges in the Southeast. Crash data documents 91 collisions at this interchange, including 2 fatal crashes and 22 people injured. Trucks navigating this interchange must execute complex merging and weaving maneuvers at highway speed while contending with passenger vehicles, construction zones, and confusing signage.

The adjacent I-20 at US-176 interchange recorded 199 total collisions, 1 fatality, and 67 injuries — further evidence that the entire corridor surrounding Bush River Road and Malfunction Junction is systemically dangerous.

Pedestrian Fatality Near Bush River Road

The danger extends beyond vehicle-to-vehicle crashes. A pedestrian was killed behind a garbage truck on Wescott Road near Bush River Road, highlighting the risk to vulnerable road users in a corridor dominated by heavy vehicles. Workers, pedestrians, and cyclists sharing space with trucks on Bush River Road's commercial strip face extreme danger from vehicles with large blind spots, long stopping distances, and wide turning radii.

Why This Corridor Is So Dangerous

Interstate Convergence

Bush River Road sits at the junction of two major interstates carrying freight traffic from across the Southeast. I-26 connects Columbia to Charleston and the port system. I-20 connects Columbia to Atlanta and Florence. Trucks transitioning between these interstates must navigate through Malfunction Junction — a maze of ramps, merges, and lane changes that requires split-second decisions at 65+ mph. One missed exit or miscalculated merge puts an 80,000-pound truck across multiple lanes of traffic.

Carolina Crossroads Construction

The Carolina Crossroads improvement project is SCDOT's massive effort to rebuild the I-20/I-26/I-126 interchange. During construction, traffic patterns shift regularly, temporary lanes replace permanent ones, barriers narrow the roadway, and construction equipment operates adjacent to live traffic. Trucks navigating construction zones face reduced sight lines, uneven pavement, abrupt lane shifts, and speed differentials — all factors that increase crash risk. Construction zone truck crashes tend to be especially severe because concrete barriers eliminate escape routes.

Bush River Road Commercial Traffic

Bush River Road itself is a commercial corridor with auto dealerships, retail centers, restaurants, and industrial businesses. Delivery trucks, fuel tankers, and tractor-trailers service these businesses while competing for space with I-26 interchange traffic. Trucks making left turns into business driveways block travel lanes and create sight-line obstructions. The mix of high-speed interchange traffic and low-speed commercial turning movements is inherently dangerous.

Common Truck Crash Types at Bush River Road & I-26

Merge and Weave Crashes

The most characteristic crash type at this location. Trucks merging from I-26 onto I-20 — or vice versa — must cross multiple lanes of traffic in a short distance. Failed lane changes and misjudged gaps result in sideswipe collisions and forced-off-road crashes. When a truck forces a passenger vehicle off the road at highway speed, the consequences are catastrophic.

Rear-End Collisions

Traffic backing up from the Bush River Road interchange extends onto I-26 mainline lanes during peak hours. Trucks approaching at highway speed encounter stopped or slow-moving traffic with insufficient warning. The speed differential between a truck traveling at 65 mph and stopped traffic produces massive collision forces.

Wrong-Exit and Confusion Crashes

The ramp closure and ongoing construction create confusion for truck drivers, especially those unfamiliar with current traffic patterns. Trucks that miss their exit attempt last-second lane changes or even reverse on ramps. GPS systems may not reflect current closures, directing trucks onto closed ramps or into construction zones.

  1. Call 911 immediately — This area may involve Lexington County Sheriff, Columbia Police, or South Carolina Highway Patrol depending on whether the crash occurs on the interstate, ramps, or surface road.
  2. Move to safety if possible — Interstate and interchange crashes create extreme secondary collision risk from approaching traffic.
  3. Document the truck: Company name, USDOT number, trailer number, cargo type, and which ramp or lane the truck was using.
  4. Note construction zone details: Which lanes were closed, what signage was posted, where barriers were placed, and whether construction workers were present.

  6. Contact a truck accident attorney — Construction zone evidence, ELD data, and the truck's event data recorder must be preserved immediately.

The moments after a car accident are disorienting. One minute you are driving, and the next you are dealing with the jarring reality of a collision. In South Carolina, thousands of crashes occur each year, leaving many unsure of what to do next. This guide provides clear, step-by-step instructions to protect your safety and your rights after a car accident in Columbia.

Immediate Actions at the Accident Scene

In the immediate aftermath of a collision, your personal safety is the only priority. Whether you are on a busy stretch of I-26 or a downtown road like Assembly Street, the first few minutes are critical. Your mind will be racing, but focusing on a few key actions can make all the difference. Before you think about insurance or blame, check yourself and your passengers for injuries. If anyone is hurt or if the vehicles are obstructing traffic, your first and most important action is to call 911.

Calling for emergency services is non-negotiable. It brings medical help to the scene and initiates an official police report, which becomes the first piece of formal documentation of the incident. While waiting for help to arrive, if it is safe to do so, move your vehicle to the shoulder to prevent further accidents. When you speak with the other driver, exchange only essential information: name, contact details, and insurance provider. It is vital that you avoid any discussion of fault. Simple phrases like "I'm so sorry" can be misinterpreted as an admission of guilt. Stick to the facts and let the authorities do their job. This is the most important first step in understanding what to do after a car accident.

Gathering Crucial Evidence and Information

Once you have addressed immediate safety concerns, your focus should shift to documenting the scene. The information you collect here forms the foundation of any future insurance claim. Think of your smartphone as your most important tool. Create a quick car accident checklist Columbia SC to ensure you do not miss anything in the heat of the moment. Start by taking wide-angle photos of the entire scene, capturing the positions of the vehicles, traffic signs, and any skid marks on the road.

Next, get close-ups of the damage to all vehicles involved. Photograph the other driver's license plate, driver's license, and insurance card. This is a foolproof way to ensure you have accurate information. While you are at it, take a moment to jot down your own recollection of what happened. Note the time, the weather conditions, and a simple narrative of the events leading up to the crash. Your memory is freshest right after the incident. An experienced attorney can later use this collection of photos and notes to build a strong case. For instance, the details you gather are precisely what legal professionals, such as those who handle complex car accident cases, rely on to reconstruct the accident and protect your interests.

Official Reporting and Medical Assessment

With the scene documented, the next steps involve official reporting and a crucial health check. The responding officer will create a police report, often known as Form FR-10 in South Carolina. This document is the primary record insurers use to begin determining fault, so be sure to get the report number from the officer before you leave the scene. You will need it to obtain a copy later.

Equally important is seeking a medical evaluation. Even if you feel fine, you should get checked by a doctor. The adrenaline from a crash can easily mask pain from serious Columbia SC car accident injuries like whiplash, internal bleeding, or concussions. As legal resource FindLaw highlights, it is essential to see a doctor because many serious injuries are not immediately apparent. Visiting an urgent care clinic or a hospital like Prisma Health creates a medical record linking any injuries to the accident. From this point forward, start a dedicated file for everything related to your health. Keep all medical bills, receipts for prescriptions, and doctor's notes organized. This paperwork is not just clutter; it is vital evidence for proving the extent of your damages in a potential personal injury claim.

Notifying Your Insurer and Understanding Coverage

After handling matters at the scene, your next call should be to your own insurance company. Most policies require you to notify them of any accident, regardless of who was at fault. This step is a key part of reporting a car accident in SC. Before you call, have your policy number and the basic facts of the accident ready. The most important rule for this conversation is to stick to the facts you know. Report where and when the accident happened and who was involved.

Avoid any speculation about fault, the extent of your injuries, or the cost of damages. Remember that this call will be recorded, and any uncertain statements could be used to challenge your claim later. This is also a good time to understand your own coverage. Your policy likely includes several key protections under South Carolina law. Collision coverage helps pay for repairs to your vehicle. Uninsured Motorist (UM) coverage protects you if the at-fault driver has no insurance, while Underinsured Motorist (UIM) coverage applies if their policy limits are too low to cover your damages. Knowing what your policy includes prepares you for the road ahead.

Navigating the South Carolina Claims Process

South Carolina is an "at-fault" state, which means the driver who caused the collision is legally responsible for the resulting damages. This is one of the most important South Carolina car accident laws to know. Because of this, you will soon be contacted by the other driver's insurance adjuster. It is their job to resolve the claim for the lowest possible amount.

Be cautious in these conversations. Never give a recorded statement to the other party's insurer or sign any documents without having them reviewed by an attorney. A quick settlement offer may seem tempting, but it often fails to account for future medical needs or lost income. It is also crucial to know that South Carolina has a three-year statute of limitations for filing a personal injury lawsuit. If you wait longer than three years from the date of the accident, you lose your right to seek compensation in court. A claim can cover more than just vehicle repairs, and understanding what you may be entitled to is essential.
Category of Damages What It Covers Examples
Economic Damages Direct, calculable financial losses caused by the accident. Medical bills, physical therapy costs, lost wages, future lost income, vehicle repair or replacement.
Non-Economic Damages Intangible losses related to the physical and emotional impact of the accident. Pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, permanent disfigurement or disability.
Punitive Damages Awarded in rare cases to punish the at-fault party for extreme negligence or recklessness. Accidents caused by a drunk driver or a driver engaging in street racing.

When to Consider Legal Help in Columbia

While some minor fender benders can be handled directly with insurers, many situations require professional legal guidance. How do you know when it is time to call for help? Look for these red flags:

  • You or a passenger suffered serious injuries.
  • The other driver's insurance company is disputing fault.
  • The at-fault driver was uninsured or underinsured.
  • The settlement offer seems far too low to cover your bills and losses.
  • You feel pressured to accept an offer quickly.

If any of these apply, you should consider speaking with a personal injury lawyer Columbia SC. A local attorney understands the nuances of Richland and Lexington County courts and has experience with local insurance adjusters. They can investigate the accident, calculate the full value of your claim, and negotiate on your behalf. Many people hesitate due to cost, but most personal injury lawyers work on a contingency fee basis. This means you pay nothing upfront, and the attorney only receives a fee if they win your case. When you decide to seek legal counsel, finding a firm with a clear point of contact is a crucial first step. Many reputable attorneys provide straightforward ways to get in touch for a case evaluation, removing any barrier to getting the answers you need.

Calling for emergency services is non-negotiable. It brings medical help to the scene and initiates an official police report, which becomes the first piece of formal documentation of the incident. While waiting for help to arrive, if it is safe to do so, move your vehicle to the shoulder to prevent further accidents. When you speak with the other driver, exchange only essential information: name, contact details, and insurance provider. It is vital that you avoid any discussion of fault. Simple phrases like "I'm so sorry" can be misinterpreted as an admission of guilt. Stick to the facts and let the authorities do their job. This is the most important first step in understanding what to do after a car accident.

Gathering Crucial Evidence and Information

Once you have addressed immediate safety concerns, your focus should shift to documenting the scene. The information you collect here forms the foundation of any future insurance claim. Think of your smartphone as your most important tool. Create a quick car accident checklist Columbia SC to ensure you do not miss anything in the heat of the moment. Start by taking wide-angle photos of the entire scene, capturing the positions of the vehicles, traffic signs, and any skid marks on the road.

Next, get close-ups of the damage to all vehicles involved. Photograph the other driver's license plate, driver's license, and insurance card. This is a foolproof way to ensure you have accurate information. While you are at it, take a moment to jot down your own recollection of what happened. Note the time, the weather conditions, and a simple narrative of the events leading up to the crash. Your memory is freshest right after the incident. An experienced attorney can later use this collection of photos and notes to build a strong case. For instance, the details you gather are precisely what legal professionals, such as those who handle complex car accident cases, rely on to reconstruct the accident and protect your interests.

Official Reporting and Medical Assessment

With the scene documented, the next steps involve official reporting and a crucial health check. The responding officer will create a police report, often known as Form FR-10 in South Carolina. This document is the primary record insurers use to begin determining fault, so be sure to get the report number from the officer before you leave the scene. You will need it to obtain a copy later.

Equally important is seeking a medical evaluation. Even if you feel fine, you should get checked by a doctor. The adrenaline from a crash can easily mask pain from serious Columbia SC car accident injuries like whiplash, internal bleeding, or concussions. As legal resource FindLaw highlights, it is essential to see a doctor because many serious injuries are not immediately apparent. Visiting an urgent care clinic or a hospital like Prisma Health creates a medical record linking any injuries to the accident. From this point forward, start a dedicated file for everything related to your health. Keep all medical bills, receipts for prescriptions, and doctor's notes organized. This paperwork is not just clutter; it is vital evidence for proving the extent of your damages in a potential personal injury claim.

Notifying Your Insurer and Understanding Coverage

After handling matters at the scene, your next call should be to your own insurance company. Most policies require you to notify them of any accident, regardless of who was at fault. This step is a key part of reporting a car accident in SC. Before you call, have your policy number and the basic facts of the accident ready. The most important rule for this conversation is to stick to the facts you know. Report where and when the accident happened and who was involved.

Avoid any speculation about fault, the extent of your injuries, or the cost of damages. Remember that this call will be recorded, and any uncertain statements could be used to challenge your claim later. This is also a good time to understand your own coverage. Your policy likely includes several key protections under South Carolina law. Collision coverage helps pay for repairs to your vehicle. Uninsured Motorist (UM) coverage protects you if the at-fault driver has no insurance, while Underinsured Motorist (UIM) coverage applies if their policy limits are too low to cover your damages. Knowing what your policy includes prepares you for the road ahead.

Navigating the South Carolina Claims Process

South Carolina is an "at-fault" state, which means the driver who caused the collision is legally responsible for the resulting damages. This is one of the most important South Carolina car accident laws to know. Because of this, you will soon be contacted by the other driver's insurance adjuster. It is their job to resolve the claim for the lowest possible amount.

Be cautious in these conversations. Never give a recorded statement to the other party's insurer or sign any documents without having them reviewed by an attorney. A quick settlement offer may seem tempting, but it often fails to account for future medical needs or lost income. It is also crucial to know that South Carolina has a three-year statute of limitations for filing a personal injury lawsuit. If you wait longer than three years from the date of the accident, you lose your right to seek compensation in court. A claim can cover more than just vehicle repairs, and understanding what you may be entitled to is essential.
Category of Damages What It Covers Examples
Economic Damages Direct, calculable financial losses caused by the accident. Medical bills, physical therapy costs, lost wages, future lost income, vehicle repair or replacement.
Non-Economic Damages Intangible losses related to the physical and emotional impact of the accident. Pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, permanent disfigurement or disability.
Punitive Damages Awarded only in rare cases, and must be proved by clear and convincing evidence (S.C. Code § 15-33-135). Accidents caused by a drunk driver or a driver engaging in street racing.

When to Consider Legal Help in Columbia

While some minor fender benders can be handled directly with insurers, many situations require professional legal guidance. How do you know when it is time to call for help? Look for these red flags:

  • You or a passenger suffered serious injuries.
  • The other driver's insurance company is disputing fault.
  • The at-fault driver was uninsured or underinsured.
  • The settlement offer seems far too low to cover your bills and losses.
  • You feel pressured to accept an offer quickly.

If any of these apply, you should consider speaking with a personal injury lawyer Columbia SC. A local attorney understands the nuances of Richland and Lexington County courts and has experience with local insurance adjusters. They can investigate the accident, calculate the full value of your claim, and negotiate on your behalf. Many people hesitate due to cost, but most personal injury lawyers work on a contingency fee basis. This means you pay nothing upfront, and the attorney only receives a fee if they win your case. When you decide to seek legal counsel, finding a firm with a clear point of contact is a crucial first step. Many reputable attorneys provide straightforward ways to get in touch for a case evaluation, removing any barrier to getting the answers you need.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to do after a car accident in Columbia?
faqs.answer: Check yourself and your passengers for injuries. If anyone is hurt or the vehicles are obstructing traffic, call 911 immediately. That single call brings medical help and starts the official police report at the same time.

faqs.question: Why does the police report matter so much?
faqs.answer: Because it becomes the neutral account of what happened, and insurers weigh it heavily. Whether the crash is on a busy stretch of I-26 or a downtown road like Assembly Street, memories diverge quickly once everyone leaves.

faqs.question: What evidence should I gather at the scene?
faqs.answer: Photographs of vehicle positions before anything is moved, damage to every vehicle, road conditions and traffic controls, plus contact details for any witnesses. Witnesses are findable in the moment and rarely afterwards.

faqs.question: Should I get medical attention if I feel uninjured?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adrenaline masks symptoms, and some injuries take days to declare themselves. A prompt medical assessment protects your health and creates the record connecting your injuries to the collision rather than to something later.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident claim in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina generally allows three years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Waiting weakens the claim well before that deadline arrives.
